write.desc: This topic covers what can be squeezed out of the mean value theorem once derivatives exist to higher order: L'Hopital's rule for indeterminate limits, Taylor's theorem as a quantitative mean value theorem with a computable remainder, and convexity, which is read off from the first and second derivatives. The points belong together because each is a direct application of Rolle's theorem or the (Cauchy) mean value theorem.

points.name: L'Hopital's rule for the 0/0 form
points.what: State L'Hopital's rule precisely for f(x)/g(x) as x tends to c when f and g both tend to 0, including the hypotheses that g' is nonzero near c and that lim f'/g' exists, and prove it from the Cauchy mean value theorem, first for one-sided limits and then for two-sided ones.
outside: one-sided limits of functions and the sequential criterion for limits

points.name: L'Hopital's rule for infinity/infinity and limits at infinity
points.what: Extend the rule to limits as x tends to plus or minus infinity (by substituting x = 1/t) and to the case where |g(x)| tends to infinity, with the infinity/infinity case either proved by an epsilon argument using the Cauchy mean value theorem on [x, y] or carefully stated, and apply it to standard growth comparisons such as (log x)/x^a and x^n/e^x.
outside: limits at infinity and infinite limits of functions

points.name: When L'Hopital's rule fails or gives no answer
points.what: Check the hypotheses before applying the rule, and recognise the standard failures: the form is not indeterminate, lim f'/g' does not exist although lim f/g does (as for (x + sin x)/x at infinity), g' vanishes near the point, or repeated application cycles without end (as for sqrt(x^2 + 1)/x).

points.name: Higher derivatives, the classes C^n and C-infinity, and the Leibniz formula
points.what: Define the n-th derivative inductively, the classes C^n and C-infinity of n times continuously and infinitely differentiable functions, give examples showing the classes are distinct (such as x^k|x|), and state and prove by induction the Leibniz formula for the n-th derivative of a product.
outside: derivative as a function on an interval
continuity of a function on an interval

points.name: Taylor polynomials
points.what: Construct the Taylor polynomial of degree n of f at a point a as the unique polynomial of degree at most n whose value and first n derivatives at a agree with those of f, and compute it for standard functions such as e^x, sin x, cos x, log(1 + x) and (1 + x)^r.

points.name: Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder
points.what: State and prove that if f is n + 1 times differentiable on an interval then f(x) equals its Taylor polynomial of degree n at a plus f^(n+1)(c)(x - a)^(n+1)/(n + 1)! for some c between a and x, by applying Rolle's theorem (or the Cauchy mean value theorem repeatedly) to a suitable auxiliary function, and see the case n = 0 as the mean value theorem itself.

points.name: Estimating errors with the Taylor remainder
points.what: Bound the Lagrange remainder by bounding f^(n+1) on the relevant interval, and use this to approximate numbers such as e, sin(0.1) or sqrt(1.1) to a stated accuracy, choosing n large enough and justifying every step of the bound.

points.name: Proving inequalities with Taylor's theorem
points.what: Use the sign of the remainder term to prove inequalities such as e^x >= 1 + x + x^2/2 for x >= 0, cos x >= 1 - x^2/2 and x - x^3/6 <= sin x <= x for x >= 0, and to show that the Taylor polynomial approximates f to higher order, so that (f(x) - P_n(x))/(x - a)^n tends to 0.

points.name: The second derivative test for local extrema
points.what: Prove that if f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0 then f has a strict local minimum at c (and the analogue for f''(c) < 0), see why the test is silent when f''(c) = 0 using x^3 and x^4, and state the higher-order version using the first nonzero derivative at c.
outside: sign of the derivative and monotonicity

points.name: Convex functions defined by chords
points.what: Define a convex function on an interval by the condition that every chord lies on or above the graph, f(tx + (1 - t)y) <= tf(x) + (1 - t)f(y), recognise standard convex and concave examples, and relate concavity of f to convexity of -f.

points.name: The slope (three-chord) inequality
points.what: Prove that for a convex function and points x < y < z the slopes of the chords over [x, y], [x, z] and [y, z] increase in that order, and deduce that a convex function on an open interval has one-sided derivatives everywhere and is therefore continuous there.

points.name: Convexity from the first and second derivatives
points.what: Prove that a differentiable function on an interval is convex exactly when its derivative is increasing, equivalently when its graph lies above every tangent line, and deduce that f'' >= 0 on the interval implies convexity, so that functions such as e^x, x^2 and -log x can be shown convex.
outside: sign of the derivative and monotonicity

points.name: Jensen's inequality (optional)
points.what: Prove by induction the finite form of Jensen's inequality f(sum t_i x_i) <= sum t_i f(x_i) for a convex f and weights t_i >= 0 summing to 1, and use it with the convexity of -log x to derive the inequality between the arithmetic and geometric means.

where.title: Spivak, Calculus
where.detail: Chapter 11 (Significance of the Derivative), including L'Hopital's rule and the appendix on convexity and concavity; Chapter 20 (Approximation by Polynomial Functions) for Taylor polynomials and the remainder

where.title: Bartle and Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
where.detail: Section 6.3 (L'Hospital's Rules) and Section 6.4 (Taylor's Theorem), which also covers the second derivative test and convex functions

where.title: Abbott, Understanding Analysis
where.detail: Section 5.3 (The Mean Value Theorems), including L'Hospital's rule; Section 6.6 (Taylor Series), including Lagrange's remainder theorem

where.title: Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis
where.detail: Chapter 5: L'Hospital's rule (Theorem 5.13), derivatives of higher order and Taylor's theorem (Theorem 5.15); exercises on convex functions
